I feel like I'm qualified to talk about this, since I am a woman in tech. Having women in tech is important, but it starts at the elementary school level. I see these numbers as telling of not enough promotion of STEM programs in school for girls or encouraging girls to pursue a science or technology program. I was an anomaly because my parents encouraged me to do science experiments and participate in science fairs and engineering programs, but most of my female friends didn't even know stuff like that existed or didn't want to do it because it wasn't "girly enough." So there is an issue with the educational system or general society telling girls that being smart is uncool or not girly. I believe that the reason why the number of women in tech has been low for so long, and is consistently lower, is that a lot of girls, as early as elementary school, learn that science isn't girly or that boys won't like them if they are too smart (if you think I'm joking, I've been told that and I'm only in my mid twenties, so it wasn't that long ago).

I've also been lucky to not have to overcome any major obstacles. But that doesn't mean that women before me didn't have to overcome those obstacles, and I respect the women older than me who entered a tech or science field despite the harassment, opposition, and belittlement. And even though I have not had to deal with harassment, opposition, or belittlement, I have had to deal with not being taken seriously or someone consistently asking the non-technical man a technical question even though they know I'm the technical person simply based on my gender. It gets tiring after a while, but it's also just part of gender stereotypes that unfortunately is still pretty common nowadays. We have a while to go before women are consistently treated as equal.

As to why having more women in tech is important...men and women have different viewpoints and different ways of approaching a problem. Encouraging diversity and multiple viewpoints can be important and even revolutionary to fixing a problem or working together in a group. I do a lot of groupwork with my team (all male members), and there are certain things I'll notice or realize or point out that 6 or 7 men (a diverse group within their gender) didn't notice. Or I'll have a different way of approaching a problem. Additionally, women have a different managerial style than men. Women interact and communicate with their subordinates differently than a man does. There have been some studies showing that women are less likely to lay off employees than men, which can lead to positive long-term economic success with the reduction of needing to hire and train a new workforce. Women are also more risk averse than men and more motivated by purpose or meaning of their work (men focus more on compensation and job titles).

Interestingly, from a survey, 70% of female leaders said that they thought women needed to hold at least 30% of senior posts in business, government, and elsewhere to be taken seriously and to influence decision making. A majority of male leaders didn't think that having a critical mass of women in senior roles mattered. (Obviously male from the response following here.) I think the crux of why there so many comments in that vein in general is because there are a few very distinct mindsets and it's often difficult to articulate the difference between the two.

First off, you have to immediately discount whatever percentage of people that are just inherently assholes -- regardless of gender. Naturally there aren't hard numbers, but for the sake of conversation let's say that's one-in-five people that are either contrarian, bigoted, deeply insecure, whatever. Similarly, we'll say maybe one in five goes out of their way to at least present as a good person, and these are the ones who avoid controversy to a fault and kind of just echo whatever the pervading narrative of what appears to be progressiveness.

The reason that topics like this are so divisive is that for that middle three of five, we're very much concerned with doing the right thing and also maintaining defensible, coherent positions on topics. Unfortunately, it's the group that doesn't really get a voice in the popular narrative. These people aren't homogeneous by any stretch; they're men, women, inbetweeners, black, white, brown, and don't have a unified political slant, but do share in common that they want to do good and want to hash it out.

This group is largely ingrained with the basic tenets of not being a dick: don't be sexist, don't be homophobic, don't be a bigot, everyone is born entitled to the same equal rights under the law, etc. We were taught to basically treat everyone like a Turing test: we make evaluations on people based on either their performance, their conversation, their actions, and generally treat people as individuals. And to us, that is good. But because of that, we aren't in the business of defining ourselves by identifying characteristics, and so we don't get representation in the popular discourse because there isn't a "team" to rally behind.

So, to bring this back to your comment, of course the people in the middle group find it very incoherent to be at once supposed to treat everyone as an individual but also make sweeping statements (for example) that a certain industry needs more of X **type ** of person. There's dissonance inherent to us in that. Of course, this boils down to the argument that certain types of people have historically been marginalized, or belittle, or harassed, or otherwise subjugated, and to correct those past mistakes there needs to be some initiatives to open opportunities to those groups of people. Again, so far in the argument, I firmly believe the vast majority of reasonable people are still on board, given the qualifying sentence prior. However, it gets heated and murky when someone who genuinely isn't sexist, racist, etc. is then told that they are contributing to the problem by existing and keeping to themselves, or not doing enough, because at that point there's this immense sense of blame that gets introduced, and whether or not it's explicitly stated there's a creeping sense that people think you're the problem if you're a male in technology. Put a breakpoint here, because this is where you get a lot of vitriol from people that can't shoulder it any more and tell everyone to fuck off and then spend an inordinate amount of time on TumblrInAction, and are now mostly confined to an echo chamber that feeds its own frenzy. Or, conversely, they glomb on to "clever" and "deep" image macros and wind up in Tumblr's echo chamber.

Usually around now in the logic is the introduction arguments about things like privilege, and the logic starts to break down because that's still broadly built around the notion of lumping people into these big categories. Please bear in mind I don't necessarily disagree with you, but with the current climate you've really got to be measured or else it's easy to fall into espousing weird positions that you don't actually agree with. It continues to get grey: do I have more or less privilege than my best friend because I'm Hispanic through my mom and middle-low income, but he's white and low-income? What about this person on the internet I'm talking to: am I being a dick, or does this guy just not get where I'm coming from because his parents never worried about losing their home? Is he a prick or did his dad hit him as a kid? Is she just patently dumb, or did she get steered away from focusing on her education?

So all of that was to give context of where I'm coming from. Sure, everyone has anecdotal evidence of girls being shooed away from sciences as children because it's not "girly" enough. But the numbers also show that women are the majority in higher education, so there's a point of contention we'd have to hash out. The modern stereotype of the "nerd" (which conveniently is now exploited to earn rich people billions of dollars) is entirely predicated on an archetype of males that were harassed and bullied and ostracized from society; until it became in vogue recently, how many beer-swigging dads were disappointed to see their son spending all of their time in books and on computers? Anti-intellectualism isn't a product of gender roles, and it's a problem but I'm not convinced that there's an argument to be made that it's tied to sex. I do agree that there are clearly differences in, like you said, certain approaches and behaviors that can be generally associated with one or the other. But the key there is generally associated, on a macroscopic scale. Again, I think this is a big tripping point for people -- there are a lot of mental gymnastics that are ultimately reminiscent of the whole "everyone is equal, but some people are more equal" tone that many of us find insidious.

Of course, at any point in all of the machinery you can easily convert a reasonable person to being one of the two ends of the one-in-five spectrum, and then you end up with comments that either are comically ignorant ("if girls performed better in STEM then we'd already be seeing more of them!") or the hilariously self-unaware ("people of color are superior to whites!").

I think the truth of the matter is more boring, which means that publications won't churn out article after article, people don't write comment after comment, and no one rallies around this sentiment (again to the money issue, because it doesn't sell): it used to be really bad, but there are more and more people who just want to be reasonable and stand on solid ground and it's getting better. It's a shame that we haven't hit equilibrium across society, and I've certainly got to keeps tabs on myself to make sure I'm not being a bad person and do everything I can to help the collective, but we've all got our own struggles. When you hear about, for example, women in technology recount how they've had to contend with obstacles in that path, I don't think anyone in the reasonable three-of-five hears that and is cheering to hear about your difficulties. But everyone has problems -- did a person get skipped over for a promotion because she's a woman, did another person somewhere else get overlooked because he's qualified but working toward it but there's a quota to fill -- and at a certain point shouldn't we focus on commending people for overcoming their circumstances instead of exhausting ourselves trying to make sure they never have to in the first place? As this massive rambling post is evidence of, when you start tracing the logic out it becomes sufficiently abstract as to be kind of a chore to even think about.

Is there still a mass market for pixel art games?

It depends on the game, if it's a rogue like then the market is pretty open to the idea already. If it's a side on platformer you might haveto put some effort into the juice to stand out. If it's a top down brawler you'll find some buyers but the market is pretty thin even if it isn't saturated. Strategy games haven't had 2d pixel art games in a long time with a lot of them spending big budgets on realistic graphics, that said the market here, while likely small, is entirely unstaturated.

If you're making a UI driven game then pixel art works really well, especially on mobile platforms, in fac a lot of the most popular mobile games use pixels styles even when they use 3d models. It's a pretty interesting trend and as much as the mobile market is massively oversaturated you'll still find some lovers of pixel art games in there, enough to put some budget into a larger game? Perhaps not, but the market is still growing so who knows.

Consoles wise you'll find a limited audience despite the lucrative aspects of the platform, with larger and larger tvs and the fact that people sit further from them you'll struggle to make pixel art work without massive effort and expenditure. It just isn't a very friendly platform for the style unless you're silling to invest the development to make it look nice and discerable at large resolutions.

The Wii U is a very good platform for pixel art and I'd encourage any developers or artists to try out a small release on there, it's only just starting to get heavily saturated and the higher energy market makes it easy to stand out and make some solid sales.

At the end of the day though the platforms of choice for pixel art games will always be mobile and PC, people sit close to them where pixel art looks best with minimum input on the developers part although you'll have to pick your game genre and task your aestetic properly to make it stand out. In such saturated markets you'll face a lot of competition from indies and AA and even some AAA companies in both pixel art styles and from similar "retro" looking art styles.
